title: The Great Unbundling, with Vincent Horn

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for modern mutants interested in mindfulness, meditation, awakening, and more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode, I'm very happy to be talking with mindfulness teacher and co-founder of the Buddhist Geeks Project, an uber-geek himself, Mr. Vincent Horn. Vince is part of a new generation of teachers translating age-old wisdom into 21st century code. In this session, Vince and I discuss the radical sense of experimentation, the great unbundling of the Dharma, ways which mindfulness practices and awareness practices can complement each other — something that's turning out to be a theme on the show lately. We also go into the perhaps greatly exaggerated reports of the death of Buddhism, as well as a scintillatingly juvenile foray into enlightened scatology. So without further ado, I give you the episode called The Great Unbundling. Hey Vince, welcome to Deconstructing Yourself. How's it going today?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I am in one piece so far.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Excellent. That's as good as anyone can hope for. How would you feel about introducing yourself to the audience?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, sure. So yeah, my name is Vince Horn and I do a lot of things. I teach meditation. I try to stay abreast of what's happening in the Buddhist and mindfulness worlds because for whatever reason, those areas have been really important to me the last decade or two. And I run a project called Meditate.io, which is a teaching project. And we basically put on virtual training programs and work with students. I say we — this is my wife, Emily, and I. I was running a podcast called Buddhist Geeks for about a decade.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: A little podcast called Buddhist Geeks that no one's ever heard of.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, people inside a very rarefied space know about it more than people outside. Usually say, that's a cool name.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right. And you also did the conference of the same name, correct?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah. So after a number of years of podcasting, it seemed like a good idea to actually meet some of these people and bring this weird group of people together. So we put on a number of in-person gatherings.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, I heard a rumor somewhere in the backwoods of North Carolina that you might be resurrecting the Buddhist Geeks podcast.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, what I've been telling people is that there's some stirrings in the bardo — meaning that liminal place between life and death. There's some activity happening. Yes, it's true.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So we're not getting a firm yes, we're getting stirrings from the bardo.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Well, it'll be, yeah, as yes as a yes can be in the liminal phase.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I think so. I mean, I'm starting to reach out to talk to people and try to imagine how this could be done and done well, including with you. Love to have you on there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Oh, great. Okay, we can trade guesting on each other's podcast. That sounds awesome. I'm curious what your background is meditation-wise, how did you get into all this, and what do you think has been the most useful practices for you leading up to now being fairly well-known and a teacher and so on?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Well, I had my first formal introduction to meditation by my Aunt Janann when I was 13. I took a meditation class with her. And so I sort of come by it honestly in the sense that my whole family — on my mom's side — has been interested in meditation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Lucky.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: As far back as I can remember, yeah, it's both lucky on the one hand, being introduced so early, and, you know, like every family religion, it has its own downsides and drawbacks as well. At least that's what I found. What I learned from her is actually now coming back around as being a really important thing, which was mostly working with awareness of the earth, bringing one's attention down into the earth and kind of combining that proprioceptive awareness down there with sort of visualization, imagining different kinds of, I don't know what you call them, like they're kind of new age meditation exercises.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I guess these earth visualizations that you're describing sound like Reggie Ray.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Exactly, and there's a strong earth awareness component. Now that I'm aware of his work and working with it myself, it's sort of bringing those memories back online.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So you're doing Reggie Ray stuff currently?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I am. The somatic body-based stuff has been the direction I've been cattle-called into by some malevolent force.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's called life.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Awesome. So what Aunt Janann got you into early on, you're finding yourself circling back to — working with the body-based practices and some, you called it, new age visualizations.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm not doing the new age visualizations as much. Not that I have anything against them either. Yeah, that introduction was helpful. And then after a number of years of just being an angsty teen, I kind of came back around to it in college and had a bit of an existential crisis, questioning, you know, what is this, what's this all about, why am I getting a degree in computer engineering, why does that matter, how much money I make, you know, those kind of questions. And that sort of led pretty quickly to an introduction with Buddhist practice, and in particular, insight meditation and vipassana practice. And from there I was hooked and gone. I was, I guess, 19 at the time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. So beyond that, what has really inspired you teaching-wise?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: So for sure the vipassana insight meditation stuff has been my spiritual home. And then also being introduced to Zen and practicing with a couple different teachers who were strongly influenced by that approach. That's really shaped the way I see things. And then also going to Naropa University — I was a student there for a number of years. And it's hard not to be influenced by Chögyam Trungpa, the person that founded that institution, rogue Tibetan teacher.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Hard not to spend a lot of time naked and drunk.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Surprisingly, I was in a very straight edge period during that time, so I don't think I even maybe had a drink or two during that time. I was more drunk on meditation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Excellent. Did you actually get a degree from Naropa?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I did, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: The feared Buddhist studies degree?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, essentially what they were teaching in the religious studies was kind of like a comparative mysticism with an emphasis on Buddhism. So it was a lot of the first-person mystical practices and perspectives from different traditions where Buddhism was very heavily in the center of that whole mix.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's such an amazing place. I actually moved to Boulder in the late 80s to go to Naropa and amusingly never actually attended, but did spend my requisite time naked and drunk.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Good, so you got the badge anyway.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I got the full transmission as far as I'm concerned.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: From what I understand, that is the transmission.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That would be true. Excellent. So I'm curious, Vince, you know, if we dig around in your background like I have done a little bit, we see things like you being honored on the smart list of 50 people who will change the world by Wired UK, and a power player of the mindfulness movement and so on. So you're very humble, but at a young age, you've had this massive influence on Buddhist practice and maybe meditation practice in general. So I'm just curious, what right now is exciting and interesting to you in that world?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I think, you know, zooming out to the high elevation view, I think what I'm most interested in and excited about is the way that the whole field is breaking apart, and how new things are kind of coalescing out of that, and how there's such a sense of radical experimentation that's starting to take root in those worlds. I'm not sure if people realize how radical it is, because in a way it's sort of what happens, I guess, when the torch gets passed to a new generation. And this generation that's starting to come into their own, which is my generation — I'm an elder millennial, so I sort of jokingly tell the young millennials, I'm your elder. But these weird young people, they just have such a different orientation than the boomers and folks that I've studied with, culturally, in terms of their relationship to technology, in terms of how they view the world and the kind of fluidity of that view. And so I think there's a lot of experimentation and a lot of interesting things happening at that point where the old systems and the old lineages and institutions are getting kind of crushed, and the jewels and the little bits and shiny pieces that are really what attracted people to them, often in the first place, are coming out and sort of being recognized in their more crystalline state, you know, and they're more unbundled or refined, potent. It's like synthesizing something out of the traditions, you know, pulling out that good, mind-bending stuff.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, so you're describing something that is, to me, quite intriguing, which is, as you said, the unbundling of these really — dare we say — precious jewels of these traditions, and breaking them out or decontextualizing them from their traditional cultural contexts and practice contexts, and maybe even then reconfiguring them and re-envisioning them in a completely different context, like a modular kind of idea where we can plug and play with a whole bunch of different practices, different outlooks, and perhaps even creating both brilliant and maybe even exquisite hybrids, and at the same time, some horrible misfires and complete failures on the way. So is there anything about that, any particular modularization or unbundling that right now is really on fire for you? Just to zoom in a little bit.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean, for me specifically, I think just the idea of starting to play with some of the core meditative elements of some of these traditions, and in particular, seeing the way in which certain types of practices aren't just embedded in one tradition, but they're embedded in multiple traditions. They're that core. Everywhere I've looked in terms of my practice life, I keep finding things like concentration practice, or certain kinds of investigation practices or inquiry, like using questions, or opening the heart, or finding these formless instructions on letting go of all technique and just being, or coming back into the body, feeling the body and being one with the body — things like that, that, you know, they're emphasized in different ways by different traditions. But the harder I looked in the Theravada tradition, the Theravada Buddhist tradition, the more I saw all these practices were there. Even the ones that were more explicit in, say, Zen or inside the Vajrayana Tibetan context, they were still in the Theravada. You just had to look really hard to find them. And so that to me is interesting, that independently — I mean, obviously with some amount of interaction — these different traditions kind of came upon, I don't want to say things that are perennial, but that they're repeating and that they're pretty persistent is interesting. And so I've been curious to just kind of play with pulling out some of those practices and almost playing with recombining them in different ways. I've sort of thought of it in terms of music. I'm not that much of a musician, but, you know, I think it's interesting when different notes are played together, you can get these new kind of harmonies — chords, they're called. And I feel like the same is true with some of these core meditative techniques, that when you kind of weave them together, they produce something that's altogether different than the individual components coming together. There's some new emergent chord, if you will, that gets strung.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now I know you and your wife Emily have been creating a course based on kind of this idea of chords, or putting together a number of these different practices. So you've been actually unbundling and then actually rolling it out to students. And I'm curious, can you give me an example of one of these chords that you feel is particularly powerful or useful or interesting or fun?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, so there's, you know, I guess there'd be like simple chords and then maybe more complex ones. And in the simple terms, I think of, you know, combining two things together. Although I know this is arbitrary in a way, to describe the core elements and how we describe things, because like every system, it's made up. But the current five elements that we're playing with: concentration, mindfulness, awareness, inquiry, and heartfulness. We've been sort of playing with combining those in different ways. And so bringing two together, I found it really interesting to play with the whole idea of mindfulness and awareness, those two together — where mindfulness, I guess, is important to say or describe, because we're using that term in a specific way. But we've been describing mindfulness as the practice of noticing what you're sensing in real time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Where there's some amount of cognitive awareness — that's the noticing part, where there's some tracking of what it is that I'm sensing. And then there's the sensory experience, which is not inherently cognitive. It's precognitive, or it's just the sensation and the feeling of the sensation. And then being able to track that in some sort of real-time way, which for me has the quality of like using a microscope or exploring particles, you know, and seeing how they're made up and how they change and how they move and where their boundaries are and things like that. Whereas with awareness, as you know, or more formless type of practice, where the point isn't to look at something but it's to be something or to be nothing. To me, bringing those two together and sort of exploring what feels like a real dichotomy at first, but which actually really bleed and weave into one another and can kind of play together — mindfulness, awareness, mindful awareness — that to me has been a really powerful one, and it seems like it's at the core of what's made the mindfulness movement so popular.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Something that I've been really interested in and excited about for the past several years is how, in our former understanding anyway, mindfulness and, let's say, awareness-type practices or non-dual type practices seemed to be utterly separate traditions. And not only traditionally separate, but in terms of what you were doing in the practice or even the outcome of the practice, they just were sides of the tracks, so to speak. And maybe you're too young, but when the neo-Advaita thing first hit in the early 90s, you know, their scathing critique of meditation and meditators and all that really emphasized the supposed difference. Back then the rallying cry, especially in Boulder where I lived for a long, long time, was, you know, anyone who was stupid enough to actually think they had to meditate was only getting in their own way and blocking their inherent realization of the always perfectly pure and absolutely complete shining awareness and enlightenment that was always and forever already there. And, you know, I'm not even exaggerating, right?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: No, no, you're being pretty kind.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. By the way, I always landed on the meditator side of that. But just because of the historical unfolding, at least in the way I experienced culture, the two things — mindfulness practices and awareness practices — were always contrasted as very different. And a few years ago, I wrote a long research paper about non-dual practices, and it eventually became a little book. But I just wanted to go into the history of them and study them and work on that a little bit. And it just really got my mind going. And after a while, I realized that mindfulness-type practices and awareness-type practices, as different as they seem, had multiple areas of contact and multiple ways that they could really reinforce and even augment each other synergistically — just pedagogically, or to put it bluntly, ridiculously — they help each other in a lot of ways. So this chord that you're describing between mindfulness practices and awareness practices, I think is super powerful and really interesting.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, likewise. You know, in the Buddhist world, they already, in a sense, have been integrated, at least by, for instance, a lot of the Tibetan systems have already kind of made space and room for both and talked about how certain ones are quote-unquote higher than others. They have their own story about the relationship between them, but they find a way to make room and space for both of them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: They do, although, as you're saying, it's kind of in a step-by-step or systematic way, and even that is not actually necessary. They can be practiced at the same time or going back and forth in one practice system.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, we could say they exist in the wave and particle form together.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Nice. And did you have any particular way that you've been exploring that — how to go back and forth with that chord, with that two-note chord?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I mean, my training on the mindfulness side was mostly through the noting meditation, Mahasi Sayadaw's noting technique. I think you talked to Kenneth Folk, who was, I think, your first guest. And Kenneth's one of my earliest meditation teachers. And that's what I learned from him.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I have no idea who that is.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: So that technique is really focused on parsing reality up into really subtle categories of experience and seeing how quickly all that's changing. For me, that practice naturally led to more formless awareness place, which is that as I kind of worked through that practice and everything started dissolving and falling apart and things were difficult and scary and I, you know, at some point just kind of let the process happen, wanting to rest and be and gently inquire into, you know, who am I? What is this? And so the one led to the other even without knowing that. And so I found that to be a powerful sequence — to start with the mindfulness practices and then to end with awareness. Almost like going to the gym and working out, you know, if you've done an intensive exercise where you kind of go really hard and then you just let go and relax completely, which most people at the gym don't seem to do. And, you know, the amount that you push and you exert, it's almost in the opposite direction one can rest. Because of that exertion, there's ability to rest more deeply. So I found with the mindfulness practice, the more actively I kind of investigate and try to really clearly see everything that's arising, the more, when I let go of that practice and just drop technique, the more of a sense of utter relaxation and just presence there is.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well said. And of course, that would point in the direction that the Tibetan tradition gives for the sequence, right? That you would start with mindfulness and end with awareness-type practices.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I find the other direction to be very useful also. If you listen to the first interview that I did with Shinzen on Deconstructing Yourself, we go into that in some detail. But in an overview kind of way, the idea is that awareness practices can be vastly deepened and clarified by getting into a vipassana-style deconstruction of their elements, which almost doesn't make sense when you come from the Advaita tradition. But having come from the vipassana end of the tradition and having experiences of non-dual type stuff, you begin to notice that there are areas that can be kind of excavated — in the corners of experience or in the edges of awareness — that remove subtle blockages, remove subtle dualities, remove subtle points of ignorance in that field of awareness, places that are stuck or holding. And of course, the traditional way would be to just kind of keep relaxing, keep just letting it be. And maybe over a long period of time, those stuck spots or hidden spots would just naturally reveal themselves or release automatically. However, I found it very interesting to bring a kind of precision and clarity that is typically fostered with vipassana practice to those areas, and notice that the awareness or wakeful quality of them can be quickly enhanced. So the sequence can work in the other way also.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, that makes sense. And this conversation and this exploration is what I get really excited about when I see the deconstruction of Buddhist meditative stuff happening, because it opens up the door to have this kind of conversation, where of course no one meditator is going to know all of the different sequences and ways of working with the mind and consciousness and the body. And yet there are so many incredible ways to do it that do have different results.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And you said it yourself, the radical experimentation is what's so fascinating. The fact that different people can go off and try this stuff out in kind of an unhampered way, or un-hidebound way, and see what they come up with. And as I mentioned, there might be a lot of dead ends, but we also can discover some really interesting stuff.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I think that's the thing about evolution — that evolution is wrought with dead ends. I mean, that's how it works. But we're building off of things and trying new things, and that's the only way we're going to find appropriate responses to our situation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, I can hear the traditional Buddhists out there. They're hearing this conversation and complaining that these combinations have all been tried before — Nalanda University, yada yada.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: You know, that's a pretty sophisticated argument.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It is. It is. You know, there's thousands of years of experimentation and they've already weeded out all these dead ends for us. So I'm curious, Vince, what you would say to that.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I mean, it's possible that you could go back through all these heaps and heaps of texts and find these things. And I think that's why studying Buddhism classically is still interesting, because there is such a huge repository of information. But it's also true that being able to find those things in a text is very different than knowing them for oneself and having done the hard work of figuring out what in that text actually was useful, and what was the sort of metaphysical framework that you also inherited with it that is potentially conflicting with your own understanding of reality, and how to square those things.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right. A lot of those practices come along with their own baggage culturally, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah. Does everyone need to go back — everyone that tries to find useful things that are probably there? You know, I'm not saying that argument isn't accurate. Do they have the time to do that excavation work and translation work to get to the point where they can then utilize it in some useful way? Probably not most people.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I certainly don't want to waste the rest of my life doing that.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Although I probably will end up wasting most of my life doing it. I think it's too late to turn back.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, and even if you were to excavate it in that way, you would then still need to try it out. And so we're sort of jumping to the trying-it-out phase. But beyond that, I'm curious if you think that there are things that we understand, or information that we have, or a wider view of cultural history and tradition and psychology and sociology that we can bring to bear that will actually allow us to discover things that have not just all been done before.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I do. I mean, I think that's where the chords — the idea of a chord — originates, you know, it's when you bring these elements together in a new way, suddenly something new emerges. There's no way to predict that if I played these three notes together they would harmonize in this way. You know, like if I were just looking at all the notes and I were studying the notes, I would not know that, because that information is not present at that level. But then to try something new, to bring new elements together, it's always going into, in my mind, exciting and dangerous territory, because we don't know, if the experiment really has never been tried, what the results will be. And I think that's where the most interesting and exciting work is to be done. But it's also quote-unquote dangerous in a sense, you know, in the same way that doing psychedelics is dangerous or going into uncharted territory is dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, perhaps the good kind of danger where something really valuable can come of it.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So you're famous for having introduced a whole generation of Buddhist practitioners to the ideas of technology. You know, Buddhist Geeks was revolutionary in really understanding how computers, the internet, podcasting, etc. could be brought to bear on an ancient practice tradition in a modern sangha and so on. But things have really changed in the last decade — one of the core characteristics of the digital age. And so tell me where you see things with all that now.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Well, I think the idea that everything has changed so much in the last 10 years is really interesting. It's an interesting point to start looking at that question of how are things different now. Because it's like, you know, the difference between algebra and calculus — and again, I'm not a mathematician either, these poor analogies. But in algebra, we're looking directly at things as they are, whereas calculus is looking at things as they're changing. And so it's almost like our world has taken that kind of leap in abstraction, where the rate of change is so out of control in so many different directions and areas that a big part of, I think, what we're grappling with — or I see myself grappling with and others around me grappling with — is what practice is in the midst of so much change. And I think this is where the experimentation is arising from. It's arising from a really deep need to figure out how are these things relevant. And I know some people's answer to that is a classical sort of fundamentalist approach where we say, okay, we're going to reconstruct the past and the past is good enough for now. They got it right back then, so this whole thing of experimenting is missing the point. The point is to unearth the wisdom of the tradition and become a fully embodied version of that. I haven't seen that working out super well for the communities and people that do it, as well.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Many parts of it are exquisitely beautiful.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, and there's so much there. I mean, there's so much. I remember talking to a friend of mine who had done a number of traditional three-year, three-month, three-week, three-day retreats.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Which is from the Tibetan tradition?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: From the Tibetan tradition. It's their kind of hardcore practice and their way of training people in being lamas and being able to carry forward the tradition. You learn all of the things that you're supposed to know. One of my past teachers called it intensive training for a non-existent job. She had done a three-year retreat too, so she knew this firsthand. I remember having a conversation with this friend, and they started to share a little bit of the practices they'd done in that retreat that could never be secularized. I'm talking practices where, in order to explore and fully understand the nature of disgust, you end up eating your own shit. And that's a formal part of the training. And so there's all these things there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: In the West.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah. And so, you know, how many Western communities are forming around that practice? None that I'm aware of. If they are, it's probably a private meetup. So there's so many interesting things there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: There's an app for that. Okay, there's a lot of beauty in the shit-eating tradition, but...

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: And there is. I have no idea what it's like to eat my own shit. I probably will learn something.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That said... I don't think there is anything else to say.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: We're having to deal with plenty of our own shit.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You found my weakness, which is poop jokes. I'm just incapacitated.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: So yeah, we have our own shit, and no less real. It's just — I think this shit we deal with, you know, in the digital world, like how do I not be totally addicted to my computer and to screens, and how do I go to sleep and not be an insomniac? Like those are really real, important questions for a number of people. Other people, you know, how do I feed myself and my children? Those are real questions as well — and different needs that people around the world are dealing with. And the digital age and what we've unleashed with sort of the network and the increasing interconnectivity of the whole mess, and the forces that have continued into that, the previous forces of industrialization and all the ideologies that came out of the Western Enlightenment — the whole thing is just crazy. And so I think the question of what is meditation now and how do we bring it to life and how does it actually make a real difference without simply being some sort of coping mechanism or a new thing to become addicted to — other addictions, you know, or at least in our minds we can justify why it's better — I think that's a really interesting and important question.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And do you have any answers or hints of answers to that question?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I mean, I feel like I've seen little bits and pieces emerge. My felt sense right now is that the answers are emerging through our relationships with one another.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes, this is where it gets quite fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Go ahead, please.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: As you know from the Wilberian world, this seems to be the missing element in many of these traditions, but particularly in Buddhism, which is such a monk- or nun-based tradition, focusing on practices that you do all alone by yourself in a cave. And that has its usefulness and its brilliance. And yet the interactive component, the human-to-human "you" space, person-to-person space, seems to have been quite neglected. Of course there's a few, but this understanding of how we are all affecting each other continuously, and how interesting that can be — not just as something we notice but something that we can actually use as a practice — is to me, at least in the Buddhist tradition, quite new.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I think so too. And just to get at how pervasive what you're saying is in terms of people's orientation and meditation being about first themselves or their own individual experience — I still to this day, even though this is something I've really tried to deconstruct and understand, almost every time that I think about meditation, I start with myself. I think about my experience and then I sort of extrapolate out. And I think what that reveals is how biased I am — and I'd say we are, because I don't think I learned this in isolation — how biased we are toward our view of reality being individual first. And then everything else being outside of that. Sure, we can be connected to people and things outside of us, but that's the primary, who we are primarily as an individual. And that, from a philosophical standpoint, it just doesn't seem like that view is holding up well right now. It's not philosophically in vogue anymore. Descartes is not the master philosopher anymore. Stuff that I've run across — and again, I'm an amateur philosopher too, amateur mathematician, philosopher, and musician — but, you know, the most interesting stuff really seems to be talking more about relationships as the primary stuff from which humans are constructed. One of my favorite philosophers, Alexander Bard, and Jan Söderqvist — they wrote a book recently called Syntheism: Creating God in the Internet Age. They kind of make a really strong philosophical argument for how who we are could best be viewed as a "dividual" — that we are our networks of relationship, not that we are these nodes in the network, but we literally arise as a result of our relations.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now you're talking. I mean, I feel like this is incredibly accurate, that the whole idea of the human being as an individual is mistaken from the get-go, and yet it's the fundamental building block of our culture and society. That idea is actually mistaken. I'm often quoted as saying half of who we are is other people. And I really see that over and over again, that we are arising in this intersubjective matrix, and the emphasis our society gives on our supposed individuality misses the point of that. It doesn't understand that we are, by nature, co-constructing reality all the time with other people and, in fact, other animals. And also misses it in the other direction too, that our own brain can be divided up, and each of those divided pieces is an individual consciousness — in the literal brain-study sense, where you can divide a person's brain in half and both of those halves independently think of themselves as individuals. So we can be divided up both ways. And I think that there's a tremendous amount to be learned there.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: I like that you say half. This is getting into the philosophical differences, I guess. But they're important, because it seems like we all have philosophies, and usually they're unexamined. And at the core of them, there's some basic fundamental beliefs about what reality is that animate everything, I would venture. And as a result of all that, it changes how we do meditation, how we think about it, what we think is valuable about it. And I've been noticing, as, again, a member of the millennials who grew up at the very tail end of the individual age, you know, the pre-internet age, and then grew up into and with the network — my sense of self feels really dual in that sense. I can relate to the individual perspective and keep coming back to it, I said, habitually almost. And yet there's something more about the network perspective that seems to be more accurately reflected in our current, you know, state of technology and how we communicate, how we relate, how our economics are structured and our politics. And so to me, a big question is how to refashion meditation for the network — for the network self, the network selves. That's a core question to me that has to be answered by any useful innovation in that space for people who are connected.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, I know we've got Kenneth Folk, both of our good friend, who is having people — what's the name of the practice where you label out loud together?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, social noting.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Social noting, yeah. So would that be an example of something that you're thinking of along these lines?

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, totally. That practice was what kind of opened my eyes to the possibility of meditation being more of an explicitly social exercise. And of course, you know, Kenneth didn't make up social meditation, but the idea of taking a practice that's been designed to be for the individual and to kind of make that leap across that boundary line is actually a really surprisingly hard leap to make, even though it seems so obvious in retrospect. Like, oh, do the technique that could be done internally and using an internal verbiage, you know, noting these experiences as they're happening — and then just do it out loud with other people. It's not a huge difference, and yet it's a world of difference. And part of that leap that he made — the path that both Emily and myself are on is, you know, how do we translate more practices like that into social techniques? Because there's a whole lot of other practices that could be done out loud or with other people that traditionally have been done silently by oneself.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, the Hindu Tantra tradition that I have a large background in does both a lot of mantra practice aloud and also even meditation practice together aloud. So it's not unknown to me. Although I will say that even in that tradition, the idea of meditating together in a group aloud was radical for that world. So some of these things only take the slightest twist, as you're saying — Kenneth's innovation of taking the typical noting practice that everyone's been doing in vipassana forever and then just doing it aloud together. Just that little twist seems like not very much, but it's actually a gigantic change and introduces all kinds of new elements and potentially new, in my opinion, new awakenings to the practice.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Totally, it does. It does have that effect. I've worked with enough people who've done that practice now to see that over and over again. Going back even further on your point, just to kind of trace that line of innovation backward — I was reading a book called The Birth of Insight a number of years ago, and it's a sort of scholarly look at how insight meditation arose in modern times. And what many people don't realize that haven't studied the stuff is that meditation, at least in the Buddhist context — for sure in the Theravada Buddhist context — is something that was reinvented in a certain sense in the 1800s and 1900s. There was not really a publicly or well-known lineage of monks practicing meditation. If they were, they weren't well-known, not documented by history. And what happened with this particular method, the noting meditation method, is it rose in Burma, in present-day Myanmar, in the late 1800s, early 1900s, in response to British colonialism. So the British had come into the southern part of Burma and had taken over. And in the north, where there were all these amazing Buddhist temples and monks who were studying the texts and preserving them and passing them along and practicing their current form of Buddhism as they knew it, something shifted. And the main shift had to do with these quote-unquote invaders, people coming in. And so one of the monks, a guy named Ledi Sayadaw, decided to start to teach everyone Abhidhamma — these like technical texts about the nature of mind and how it works and how it functions. And in a way, he did this so that the knowledge could be distributed, and it wasn't like the British could come and, whatever, take the monks away and then it's lost. And yet the effect of that is that out of teaching lay people these things that had been previously reserved to monks, it opened up this attitude of like, well, we can teach them this stuff too, this interesting thing I read in this text that I've been trying to do. And, you know, they ended up — out of a result of all this — the noting meditation arose as a translation of what was written down in another text called the Visuddhimagga, an older commentary on the path of meditation. And so every one of these things has been not a huge difference — I mean, I guess that's big in a certain way for them culturally — but have involved changing how one does the thing that one is faithful to, and thus changes it in the process, and yet there's some thread behind it that goes back. There's something common to social noting as there is to what's described in the Visuddhimagga. There's a relationship still there, even though it's changed a number of times now.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, so as we look at this unbundling, some people see that as the natural ebb and flow of how spiritual traditions and maybe specifically Buddhist tradition has always functioned. That these traditions remake themselves over and over again to be relevant. Obviously, that has occurred dozens, maybe even hundreds of times in the long history of Buddhism in various countries. And yet there's another opinion about this that I hear more and more, especially in the wilds of the internet, which is that this means that Buddhism as a tradition actually is dying or is dead, and that it's being cut up and rendered. And people are finding, as you mentioned, special, beautiful practices in there, but they're then being radically decontextualized and reformed into something that is perhaps completely unrecognizable as Buddhism as a tradition, or even as spirituality at all. And I'm curious if you have an opinion about that or a viewpoint on that.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Well, I would agree that Buddhism is dying, in the sense that every institution that's carried forward important human knowledge is dying. Because this unbundling force is not just happening to Buddhism. It's happening across the board with all human knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes. Sometimes it's called the great unraveling.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Every institution that basically had bundled some of our best stuff — these are the good hits — they're getting pulled apart and reconfigured and mashed up with other streams of knowledge that maybe hadn't been connected with before. And I think that's, of course, the most interesting, exciting part of this: that the boundary lines that we'd previously drawn in the modern age are falling apart, and so there's new possible configurations that can come from that. But it's also true that, yeah, there's something that's being lost. And as you say, it's not something that we're just now losing. It's something that's constantly having been lost. Old, temporarily stable knowledge bases, communities of practice, relationship structures, cultural matrices — all of that coming together in a particular time and place and working for a while. And then when the time and place or the conditions that supported it change — which, by the way, Buddhism as a tradition talks about endlessly, this process — then it changes. Buddhism changes. Something dies and then something seems to take its place, or something new comes online. So, you know, I sort of take the position of, yeah, there's birth and death. This is nothing new. And what's being born right now is unique and different because our time is unique and different. But there's also something that's not changing about this basic process of birth and death, of how, you know, something comes into being, it's beautiful, it serves things for a time or it serves its function, and then it changes, it goes away. You know, people grieve. They feel like we're screwed. The golden age of enlightenment is over. And then a few towns down, 10 years from then, some amazing thing happens. Some person's born. A new prophet comes into the world, whatever. And they share some new good news. That's better news. So, you know, in a way, like, I think it's just, yeah, whatever. Let the thousand flowers bloom. Yeah, my dad said that "whatever" is my generation's "fuck you." So take it as you will. I have heard that as well, the story you brought up. It's like, well, it's dying. And it's like, yeah, it's really painful for something I love to die. And yet that's not what Buddhism professes to be about anyways, holding on to things. Like, give me a break. If you really want to deal with these things seriously, then why not bring to bear some of the wisdom of the very thing that you're mourning to the situation? And then it's not totally dead. Then it's alive again. Whatever. That would be my response.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thanks. I work with a lot of Silicon Valley executives and high-level tech folks who don't even believe that they're going to die someday, you know. Literally. Literally, like that their physical bodies will be able to be prolonged indefinitely as long as they don't get in an accident of some sort. They'll just be conditionally immortal. And many of those people also believe they may be massively augmented by AI of various sorts. Some of them are in fact quite fearful of the apocalyptic AI future, but others believe they will be augmented or have various pals around who are artificial intelligences. And it's quite fascinating to see how this view, which in one way metaphorically is like a completely magical view — something that you could find in Tantrism a thousand years ago if you thought of the sort of magic version of it, immortality and, you know, these disembodied intelligences or non-human intelligences — but which now seem to, at least for some people, they believe they are on the verge of coming into manifest reality in a technological form. And I just can't imagine anything that would affect one's life or one's spiritual practice more than believing that you wouldn't die and that you would be actually augmented by some kind of artificial intelligence so that you have superhuman cognitive abilities. And so to me, we're dealing with a time and a place and a culture — and again, this comes back to the whole intersubjective question here of the practices — that is rife with these super intense possibilities, extreme danger, and at the same time almost inconceivably wild imaginative leaps that are on the verge of potentially becoming real. And I just am so stoked about the types of practices, the types of understandings that we're leaning into here as opening up towards that future.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Nice. I'm glad you are.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You know, I know I'm just raving here, but in other words, it's not that I think that that particular future will happen, but that this isn't some science fiction scenario in terms of the fact that, like, you and I know people who think that way every day. And they're coming to, certainly to me, and asking to be taught to meditate. And they want to understand their own minds so that in this infinite future that they are imagining for themselves, they can have a source of wisdom. I'm not sure how this is leading up to a question, except that I want to see if you have anything to say along the future-of-technology aspect of this — the way that our rapidly, rapidly changing world is creating new possibilities for awakening.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: What you're sharing immediately reminded me of reading Ray Kurzweil's book, The Singularity Is Near, when it came out in 2005. This was 12 years ago, and I was really getting into his predictions about the future of information technology and the way that that was going to impact society. And now he's at Google, of course. He's director of engineering at Google, and he's actually helping build those things that he was at that point forecasting. And it's pretty outrageous stuff. And what I've been surprised about these years later, looking back at his forecasting and the way that he did it, is that he was pretty much right on the money. Now, whether or not that holds out for the next decades, because there's some big leaps that would have to happen. Quantum computing would have to become a normal thing. Artificial intelligence, general AI, would have to become a real thing, and then AI would have to start somehow improving itself really fast. Nanotechnology and all of the barriers to having a really workable, mature nanotech and biotechnologies — that hasn't been solved. And there's so many requirements in terms of, for instance, quantum computing: the ability to have that type of paradigm-shattering new computing platform is required for so many of these other things to come true. And yet, like you say, there's so much that's happening and has been happening, and it seems like the trajectory is in that direction. So we might reach some sort of physical limitation or something and not be able to go beyond that, I'm not sure. But it seems like we're just — even now — still unlocking the ramifications of the physics of over a century ago. And so, yeah, I don't think meditation is one of the last areas to be really touched by that, touched by the work that Einstein and others did.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Niels Bohr.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: It's like we're just now coming around. We're like the most conservative people in existence. But I'm excited too. I'm more cautiously optimistic now than I've ever been about it. When I was reading that book, I was like hype. I called myself a Buddhist transhumanist for a while at that time. And now, kind of with some more space, distance — unfortunately not living in Silicon Valley, no offense — I feel like I've got some distance from the faith-based elements of that view. It seems like there's a fundamental faith in that the core of what life is, is information, and matter is simply like a computing substrate for that information. That is obviously a really powerful way of looking at reality and it opens up so many potentials. But it also feels like it restricts some aspect of what life is that can't be reduced to information. And I'm not sure exactly how to talk about that beyond just saying what I said. But part of what to me has been so interesting about some of the contemplative and mystical traditions is the way in which they point to what we don't know — how authoritatively they point to not knowing, and to how vast things are outside of the world of our concepts. And I wonder, you know, to what degree that's being overlooked in the rush to digitize enlightenment.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I think it's being almost completely overlooked from what I can tell.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: The thing that I've been so transformed by and deeply moved by is the way that meditation makes the unknown the place of experience, and it makes it home. That kind of mysterious unknown becomes very welcome and very fresh and new. And what I don't see in the Silicon Valley world is an understanding of that. There's a, as you rightly characterize it, a kind of religious belief in tearing everything apart into knowns and being able to then hack our brains to kind of get off eternally and, you know, at some kind of future Burning Man on the moon. And I don't see anyone in that world really feeling their way into this kind of — just to put it paradoxically — familiarity with the unknown, or let's say love of not knowing, which is, as far as I can tell, where all the juice is in spirituality.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Hmm. This sort of gets into kind of fuzzy territory to talk about, because I feel like I don't quite have a way of making sense of what I'm about to say. But I've sort of found also in what you're describing, Michael, where the juice is of not knowing, the unknown — it feels also kind of like an orientational shift in terms of how one knows. Like how I know now, or the process of knowing, seems to arise very much from the not knowing. That when I drop the sense of being clear, certain about how things are — at the right time, say that, at the right time — then, and can sit in the discomfort of that, or just be, you know, walking around uncomfortable and blaming it on my wife.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Sorry, honey. Somehow there is new knowing that arises, but it's tempered by that lack of certainty. It's like seeing a pattern emerge out of the amorphous space, rather than thinking really hard and having a good idea, you know, and being able to somehow take credit for that. It's more like I kind of exhausted all the bad stuff and then was open enough to see something new. I have a feeling this is kind of how creativity works, probably generally for humans, whether or not they make sense of it that way.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, this is a restatement of standard creativity theory from Wallas onward, where that third step out of four steps of the creative process is to let go of trying to solve the problem and just refocus on something else. And then later coming back to it and realizing that an insight has arisen from the unconscious, right? Just letting this not knowing, or letting a non-focusing on the problem, be the way that you solve it.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And in Buddhist tradition, this is characterized as prajna, you know, the wisdom mind — this kind of Manjushri sword of wisdom that just arises out of emptiness.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Which is kind of a beautiful metaphor, beautiful model for how that works. The thing about it is, that's a great way to solve problems. In fact, it is. And yet for me, the other way of looking at it — and again, for me, the juicier or more satisfying way to look at it — is that's also just a great place to hang out without even trying to use it to solve any problems. That kind of just a stream of pure confusion, you might call it, just hanging out with the unknowing, is tremendously pleasant. And also — the only time I'll allow myself to use a bunch of cliché spiritual metaphors about spontaneity or sahaja-type feelings — when you just allow the mind to relax into complete unknowing, there's a sense of pure freshness and spontaneity that is extremely pleasant. So I see it as being a good thing in its own right. And yet it also — it's good in itself, and yet it also, as you point out, is wonderful for creativity and problem solving.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, I imagine that for people that tend toward annihilation — which, listening to your conversation with Kenneth, the second episode, I believe it was, The Cosmic Choke, I immediately noticed that you guys both had that tendency. You're like, how can anyone be so worried about death? Like, death is great. I'm on the other side of that spectrum, where I tend toward, you know, in Buddhist parlance they called it craving for becoming — like wanting to become something new, or like loving to see what new emerges out of that stream of confusion. And so acknowledging that what you say could be true, it hasn't been my experience so much. I don't like resting in confusion. I like to get to the end where the confusion morphs into something else. But yeah, I see it's really important. And maybe another dimension of this, which is also at play here for me, is the sense that when a solution does arise from that place, it could be just as easily said, or maybe more easily said, that the problem solved me instead of me solving it. And that's where I get really fascinated with the intersection between meditative approaches that go there, that bring people into a firsthand experience of de-centering the reference point and sort of getting in touch with the phenomenology of not knowing and what emerges from quote-unquote the unconscious — what the fuck is that? Where it gets really interesting is bringing that to bear on approaches like Silicon Valley's basic approach, which is problem solving. How do we solve this problem, solve this problem? Anywhere there's a problem to be solved, there's a new product to be created and marketed. And so what would it mean for people to have problems solve them instead of them solving the problems? There's a felt sense of difference when one makes meaning in that direction, as opposed to thinking like I'm the one that's going to go change the world.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, this is what I feel like we're both pointing to — is that there's a kind of pregnant possibility inside the problem itself that is in fact the solution, that does point towards something incredibly important and awakening. And it's that shift of stance from I'm solving the problem to the problem solving me that is the crucial move there. And it's the one that, in my own anecdotal experience, I'm not seeing so much happening in the Silicon Valley world. And it might be one of the major things we can contribute to that world is helping them to feel comfortable in these places of creative possibility that involve the discomfort of confusion or not knowing.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, and even not knowing who I am, where I come from, where I'm going, anything.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: All of those tend to cause tremendous discomfort for people who are used to solving problems. And yet when the stance gets switched around to the problem solving you, those very questions are the ones that fill you with the most aliveness and creative possibility.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: And dread. Exquisite dread. You used the term non-duality earlier. And I thought back to a conversation I had with a Zen teacher named David Loy, who I was working with. I was at that time really crystallizing the sense that there wasn't a non-duality, that there really were these different types of non-duality people were talking about. But I wanted to see what he thought about that, and this kind of was my test for him. And I said, you know, do you think there are different types of non-duality? And he said, well, there are as many types of non-duality as there are dualities. And I found that to be really helpful, because it sort of was a statement about how the mind works, or how we tend to feel that there is a problem between two things and then get locked into a struggle with those two things. And at some point, we might see that there's actually not as big of a struggle or a fundamental problem as we assumed to begin with. That's really interesting, because there's so many problems. There's so many things that, you know, there's so many issues that arise being humans. And presumably people in Silicon Valley, just like any industry, are trying to solve some of those problems. Maybe they're solving old problems in new ways. But still, there's a sense that there are usually two things that are at odds and we can't square them. And it feels like somehow if I could square these things — like for a long time for me it was the vipassana versus what at the time I was calling non-duality, like the pure awareness approach. That was a real problem for me for a number of years, and then it ceased to be a problem. So yeah, I'm curious about looking at non-duality from that vantage, because then there's a lot we know already from the meditative traditions about how to work with polarities and opposites. There's different ways of working with them. I hate to go back into the solutionism, but really meditation does have a lot to offer coming up with solutions, if that's how one is using it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It absolutely does. I'm not saying in any way that those creative solutions aren't there and that they're not valuable. They are invaluable. I just wanted to emphasize that even previous to the solutions, it's already valuable.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, for sure. You know, that's a different viewpoint that seems like it can come online after letting go quite a bit. Sometimes it can just happen all at once, but usually that's at a Burning Man.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so I've been quite interested in your teaching programs. I know that you're in the midst of changing them, but if there's anything you want to describe here or plug, this is your opportunity to talk to my vast audience about that.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: So Emily Horn and myself — this is my wife and teaching partner — we do most of our teaching together and sort of bounce off of each other quite a bit. And it leads to an interesting synergy. You talked about your blogging partner and how different you all's approach is, and yet it sounds like there's something really beautifully synergistic in it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Mindfulness and sex, for instance, bringing those two together.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: We're sort of in a constant process of iteration and figuring out what's working and what's not. I feel like that's part of the challenge of teaching meditation right now: that while there are models emerging and while people are taking old models and just quote-unquote putting them online, most of the exciting work seems to me needs to be done in terms of not just innovating on how meditation is taught, but also innovating on the very structures of how it's practiced together. You know, the business models and the virtual connections and how that works, and how we do social meditation on a Zoom video hangout in breakout rooms, you know, how we do it in virtual reality rooms soon. Like those questions, to me, don't have clear answers yet. And so I find a frustrating amount of time is spent really trying to experiment with and find out what would be really useful for people. So we've been in a process of that for the last couple months that we're just coming out of. And to our — not total surprise, but a little bit surprise — we found that the people that are tuning into what we do with Meditate.io really are very hyper-independent in their orientation. Like, they're DIY extreme. And I think there's something about that orientation to learning that really is beautiful, and we want to kind of cater to that. But at the same time, you know, it can go off the rails, in the sense that people get overconfident in what they know and what they can know by themselves. And so our first thing that we've done recently is to start offering our time in the form of teacher meetings with people, so that they can get access to yet another couple of trained teachers and talk about their practice. And to me, this is like the biggest bang for the buck. I know you do this work, Michael, with people. In terms of practice and working one-on-one with someone where you end up clicking and there's like good healthy boundaries — that's been the most ROI, you know, you could say in terms of time, it's the most return on investment. Being able to learn from another person, with another person, is just huge. So that's what we're doing now, and then we've got some other things, but they're not kind of formed yet.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: All right, Vince, very good to talk to you. I've been dying to do this for a long time, so thanks.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, thank you for having me.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, and I look forward to hearing the hopeful rebooting of Buddhist Geeks.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Oh, thank you. Yeah, me too.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: All right, have a good one.

transcript.speaker: Vincent Horn
transcript.text: Yeah, you too.
